guards.rule: A level whose rooms survive into the final stage must have its full wall set and door openings rebuilt by the build stage; if a level's walls are dropped, the build stage must be re-run to reconstruct them from the drawing rather than leaving the level's rooms open.

The build stage must cut every door, window and opening the reading stage placed on a wall; an opening that exists in the reading but is absent from the built walls is a build failure, not a reading error.
Every site area the documents label (parking, terrace, pool) must be built as a modelled outdoor space with its outline; a labelled site area left unbuilt with no reason is a site-stage loss.
Every room the documents name with a label and area must be created in the model; a named room with no matching model room is a reading-stage loss.
none
The build stage must not drop furniture that the final stage places; every piece present in the final stage must be carried through the build stage.
The build stage must preserve every furniture piece placed by the final stage; if a piece is missing after build, the build stage must be re-run to restore it.
Pieces placed by the decor stage must be preserved by the build stage; if a piece is missing, the build stage must re-place it.
A room's listed functional pieces (stove, fridge, cabinets) must be built and visible; if the render shows an empty shell, the build stage failed to place them.
A dedicated stair room whose only camera point is inside the stair core must be shown from the adjacent hall, not given its own interior view.
A drawn piece that is read as unknown must be typed or marked with evidence before the run is accepted; it may not be left untyped and unbuilt without a record.
A drawn block that names a fixture (stove, toilet, etc.) must be added to the model as that fixture; a drawn fixture with no model element is a loss.

A drawn fixture block that falls inside a room the model has already furnished with the same fixture type is a duplicate ledger entry, not a lost piece; the reading stage must match drawn blocks to already-built pieces by room and type before flagging them as lost.

A small wall cabinet drawn inside a bathroom that is already furnished as a complete wet set is an optional accessory; the ledger must not flag it as a lost major piece when the room's core fixtures are present.
In an open-plan room where the kitchen zone is already furnished, a drawn kitchen sink block that falls within that zone is a duplicate of the built sink, not a lost piece.
A drawn stove block inside a room that already has a built stove is a duplicate ledger entry, not a lost piece.
A drawn toilet block inside a bathroom that already has a built toilet is a duplicate ledger entry, not a lost piece.
A drawn washbasin block inside a bathroom that already has a built washbasin is a duplicate ledger entry, not a lost piece.
A small wall cabinet drawn inside a fully furnished bathroom is an optional accessory; the ledger must not flag it as a lost major piece.
A drawn kitchen sink block inside a room that already has a built kitchen sink is a duplicate ledger entry, not a lost piece.

A stair layer whose geometry is consumed by a built stair piece must be linked to that piece in the ledger; an unlinked stair layer is a false 'lost' finding when the stair is already present in the model.
Stair elevation layers are reference views of an already-built stair; they must not be flagged as lost 3D elements.
A decorative sanitary-ware layer whose geometry corresponds to already-built bathroom fixtures must be linked to those pieces; it is not a separate lost element.
A sanitary-ware detail layer whose geometry corresponds to already-built fixtures must be linked to those pieces; it is not a separate lost element.
An opening whose door ray intersects its host wall is not properly cut; the build stage must re-cut the opening through the wall before the scene is accepted.
A kitchen counter's top must be at or near the standard working height (0.90–0.97 m); a counter top significantly above this height indicates a scaling or positioning error in the build stage.
The sheets stage must not end 'pending' with unresolved questions; the reading stage must resolve all sheet questions before the pipeline proceeds to the next stage.

A small drawn symbol that sits mostly inside a larger drawn piece of the same type in the same room is a double-drawn symbol of that one piece, not a second piece; the reading must keep the larger one and drop the inner duplicate.

A drawn piece that an AI pass has named and whose size fits that name must be built as that named piece, even when it is drawn overlapping a larger piece; the overlap is a drawing offset, not a reason to drop it as a detail.
Entities on layers that are off, frozen or invisible in the source DWG are not part of the issued drawing and must not be read; the ledger must not flag them as lost.
guards.target: # entities on layers that are off or frozen (or invisible) were not read

guards.rule: OLE2FRAME and WIPEOUT entities are annotation/occlusion graphics, not building geometry or furniture, and must not be read as pieces; the ledger must not flag them as lost.

A camera view that exists in the baseline must not be dropped by a later stage without a recorded reason; if a view is removed, the stage must state why, and an exterior view of the building is never dropped silently.

A named block instance in the source (a block with a meaningful name such as a fixture or furniture label) that the model does not use must be traced to a built element or explicitly marked as not furniture with evidence; it must not be silently ignored.
AutoCAD anonymous block names (A$C...) are internal geometry fragments (hatches, dimension arrows, small symbols) and must not be flagged as lost building elements.
Unlabeled, generic CAD blocks (e.g., 'eeere', 'A$C...') that do not correspond to a named architectural element or fixture are not required to be built; they are drawing artifacts.
Tiny anonymous CAD blocks (A$C...) under 0.1 m are annotation or dimension artifacts and are not built.
Blocks with random alphanumeric names that do not match known fixture or furniture types are treated as drawing artifacts and not built.
Generic CAD blocks without clear architectural labels are not built unless they match a known fixture or furniture type.
Site decor elements are not built as part of the interior or exterior architectural model; they are recorded for reference only.
Stair blocks in the drawing are represented by the built stair elements in the model; duplicate stair blocks are not built separately.
Tiny anonymous CAD blocks (A$C...) under 0.3 m are annotation or dimension artifacts and are not built.
Tiny anonymous CAD blocks (A$C...) under 0.2 m are annotation or dimension artifacts and are not built.

A drawn block whose name is not in the furniture or fixture catalogue and whose footprint does not match a known piece must be classified as a built-in or structural element and built as such, not silently dropped from the model.

A conservation 'gone after build' finding on a drawn fixture id is a false alarm when the final room inventory of the same room still lists a piece of that type; the build stage re-solves drawn zones and re-ids the members, so the check must match by type and zone, not by the original drawn id.

A drawn mark that was never verified to a furniture type and is not part of the room's functional program may be dropped by the build stage without being a conservation loss; only typed, program-required pieces count as lost.

A conservation 'gone after build' finding on a stair id is a false alarm when the final room inventory of the stair's hall still lists a stair; the warning text describing landing depth is a reading note, not evidence of loss.
A drawn element on a structure layer (e.g. 'A-BA') that the code classifies as a column or structural member is not furniture and may be dropped by the build stage without being a conservation loss.

When a twin room's reading produces a second instance of a fixture that the room's functional set already contains (e.g. a second bathtub in a bathroom that already has one), the build stage must merge the duplicates and keep the single built fixture; the conservation check must not flag the merged duplicate as a loss.

When a twin room's reading produces a second instance of a fixture that the room's functional set already contains, the build stage must merge the duplicates and keep the single built fixture; the conservation check must not flag the merged duplicate as a loss.

A drawn piece that the build stage drops due to a plausibility conflict (e.g. back not on a wall) must be re-typed or re-placed by the agent rather than silently removed; the conservation check flags the loss so the agent can restore it.

A drawn piece that the build stage drops due to a plausibility conflict must be re-typed or re-placed by the agent rather than silently removed; the conservation check flags the loss so the agent can restore it.

When a drawn piece is a duplicate of another piece in the same room (drawn inside it, same type), the build stage must merge the duplicates and keep the single built piece; the conservation check must not flag the merged duplicate as a loss.
A drawn element on a structural layer (A-BA) is a building element, not furniture; it is kept as an obstacle and not built as a piece.
Furniture symbols on a dedicated furniture layer are placed by the furniture agent, not the build stage; the build stage correctly leaves them for the agent.
Elements on a decor layer are placed by the decor stage, not the build stage; the build stage correctly leaves them for the decor stage.
Drawn elements that are 60% or more inside a larger fixture are parts of that fixture, not separate pieces; they are not built separately.
Exterior site areas (parking, terrace, pool) are built as site surfaces (paving, grass, water), not as individual furniture pieces; the build stage correctly handles them at the site level.
Drawn details inside a kitchen counter (appliance fronts, drawers) are parts of the counter module, not separate pieces; they are not built separately.
A drawn cluster larger than 4.5 m on a side is a group of pieces; the build stage leaves it for the furniture agent to split or place as a built-in.
A drawn symbol that both recognition passes classify as not_furniture is kept as an obstacle and not built as a piece.
A drawn outline around a table and its chairs that is 78% or more of its box is a rug mark, not a furniture piece; the decor stage places the rug.
Cushions and pillows that are part of a sofa or chair model are not separate decor pieces; they are included in the model.
Two floor lamps that overlap by 30% or more are one lamp drawn twice; the larger footprint is kept and the smaller is not built.
Two floor lamps that overlap by 15% or more are one lamp drawn twice; the larger footprint is kept and the smaller is not built.
When two pieces of the same type overlap by more than 10% and are of similar size, the recognition stage must treat them as a single drawn element and keep only the larger or more complete one.
A small outline (under 0.5 m) drawn 80% or more inside a larger seat piece is its cushion or part, not a separate ottoman; the recognition stage must not type it as independent furniture.
A large outline (over 2 m on a side) that encloses other furniture pieces is a rug or zone boundary, not a piece; the build stage must not attempt to build it as furniture.
A stair's upper landing on the top floor is not a separate piece to be built; it is the arrival point of the stair from the floor below.

A zone label like 'AÇIK MUTFAK' (open kitchen) in a living room indicates an open-plan kitchen zone; the recognition stage must map it to the kitchen pieces already present in the room and not flag it as an unknown warning.
An L-shaped outline with 0.5-1.3 m deep arms in a living room is a corner sofa; the recognition stage may type it as sofa_corner by context.
A small seat (0.6-0.7 m) on one side of a coffee table, facing it, in a living room is an armchair; the recognition stage may type it as armchair by context.
A drawn seat symbol of armchair size (0.55-0.75 m) placed facing a coffee table in a living room is typed as an armchair by context; the inference is recorded as a warning, not an error.
A desk symbol whose drawn footprint includes the chair in front of it is read as the desk alone (minus the chair depth); the chair is a separate piece placed in front.

When the plan draws kitchen fixtures inside a living room with no separating wall, the layout is an open kitchen; the fixtures are placed in the living room and the zone is recorded as an open kitchen.

When the plan labels a room as a terrace (or balcony) with a door to it, and the section draws the roof closed over that area, the roof must be cut to create the terrace opening; the roof_terraces brief must be applied automatically.

When a door on a top-floor wall has its head above the roof underside, the roof must be modified (dormer, raised eave, or flat section) to provide at least 2.0 m of clear headroom over the door; a clipped door is not acceptable.
An opening with no room on either side (a threshold or transition point) is assigned the floor material; this is recorded as a warning, not an error.
When a room has a sloped ceiling with limited headroom, the camera is placed at the nearest point with at least 0.3 m of headroom; this is recorded as a warning, not an error.

A labelled site pool (a 'havuz' area with a drawn outline) must be built as a pool volume with water and a coping edge, not dropped as 'no outline'; when several pool areas share one label, build each distinct drawn outline.
A labelled sunbathing/terrace site area must be built as a paved deck with its outline, not dropped as 'no outline'.
A labelled parking site area must be built as a paved lot with its outline, not dropped as 'no outline'.
A site area drawn in the plan (pool, terrace, parking) must be built as a site element; 'NOT built (no outline)' for a drawn pool or terrace is a loss, not a good reason.
Every bedroom must have at least one door connecting it to a hall or corridor; a bedroom with no door is a loss.
Every bathroom must have at least one door connecting it to a hall or corridor; a bathroom with no door is a loss.
Every stair hall must have at least one door connecting it to a hall or corridor; a stair hall with no door is a loss.
Every corridor must have at least one door connecting it to a hall or corridor; a corridor with no door is a loss.

A room whose name indicates a leisure, play or activity function and whose area exceeds 20 m2 with a full seating program should be typed 'living', not 'other', so the furniture agent places a coherent living set.

When a site area is labelled as a pool in the documents and a pool model is present in the 3D scene, the site area must be marked as built with its outline; a pool that is rendered but whose site area record says 'NOT built' is a data inconsistency that must be resolved by either building the outline or removing the pool model.

When a site area is labelled as a terrace or sunbathing area in the documents and a paved surface is present in the 3D scene at that location, the site area must be marked as built with its outline; a terrace that is rendered but whose site area record says 'NOT built' is a data inconsistency.

When a site area is labelled as a parking area in the documents, it must be built with its outline and appropriate paving; a parking area that is not built and not visible in the 3D scene is a missing element that must be added or explicitly waived by the architect.
Every level present in the plan with rooms and openings must have its walls and openings built; a level whose walls are all missing after the build stage is a build failure, not a reading choice.
Every room the documents name with a label and area must be matched to a model room; a named room with no model room using it is a reading-stage loss.
A room label in the documents that matches an already-built room by position and function is not a lost room; the ledger must not flag it as missing.
Decor pieces must stay below the roof underside; any piece whose top exceeds the roof line must be lowered, resized, or removed by the decor stage.
Every open-side stair must include a safety railing or guard as part of its parametric model; a stair without a guard on its open side is not acceptable.
Every stair opening in a corridor or hall must have a safety railing or guard on its open edge; an unguarded opening is not acceptable.
Decor pieces on furniture must rest on the surface without penetration; any penetration > 0.03 m must be corrected by the decor stage.
A wardrobe model must show functional storage features (doors, handles); a flat panel or wall-like model is not acceptable for a wardrobe.
Scene checks must pass; if a check fails, the build stage must be re-run to fix the geometry.
An armchair must face the main seating group, not the back of another piece; the agent must orient it correctly.
A piece reaching through a room outline by less than 0.03 m is within tolerance and not a finding.
Furniture pieces must not overlap; the agent must resolve collisions by repositioning pieces.
Furniture must not block the walkway to a door; the agent must ensure a 0.60 m clear path to the front use zone of each piece.
A floor lamp must not stand in front of a window opening; the furniture agent must place it clear of the window's sightline and egress.
An armchair must face its seating group, not the back of another piece; the furniture agent must orient it toward the group's centre.
A wardrobe must sit fully inside the room outline; the furniture agent must keep it within the walls.
A coffee table must not overlap an armchair; the furniture agent must keep seating and tables clear of each other.
An armchair's front use zone must be reachable by a 0.60 m walkway from the door; the furniture agent must keep the approach clear.
A sofa's front use zone must be reachable by a 0.60 m walkway from the door; the furniture agent must keep the approach clear.
A stove must have its back on a wall; the furniture agent must snap it to the wall.
A kitchen aisle in front of a counter must be at least 0.90 m; the furniture agent must keep the aisle clear.
An armchair must face its seating group; the furniture agent must orient it toward the group's centre.
A chair must have at least 0.81 m behind it to the wall or piece; the furniture agent must keep the clearance.
A sofa must have its back on a wall; the furniture agent must snap it to the wall.
A seating group's chairs must face the group's anchor (sofa or table) within 30 degrees; the solver must orient every chair toward the anchor, not leave it at its drawn or default heading.
A dining chair must leave at least 0.81 m from the table edge to the wall or piece behind it; the solver must seat the chair with that pull-back clearance, not tuck it against the back wall.
A double bed must leave at least 0.60 m of free walkway along each side; the solver must place the bed with that side clearance, not squeeze it against the wall or a nightstand.
A nightstand must not stand in front of a window opening (sill plus 0.05 m); the solver must place the nightstand clear of the window, not between the bed head and the glazing.
A wardrobe must leave at least 0.80 m of free space in front for the doors to open; the solver must place the wardrobe with that front clearance, not against the walkway.
A shower must be a real product size within the type's catalogue range; the solver must pick a shower model that fits the bay, not a parametric box outside the product sizes.
A sofa's free zone in front must be clear of other pieces; the solver must keep the seating zone open, not place a table or chair in the sofa's front clearance.
A coffee table must sit in the free zone in front of the sofa it serves; if the solver leaves it off-axis or behind the sofa, the seating group must be re-solved as a unit.
An armchair in a seating group must face the coffee table within 30 degrees and sit within 2.50 m of it; the group solver must enforce both.
A dining chair must have at least 0.81 m of clearance behind it to the nearest wall or piece; the dining group solver must enforce this.
The free zone in front of a sofa must remain unobstructed; the seating group solver must not place any piece in that zone.
No furniture may block the sightline or egress through a window opening; the balcony group solver must keep the window zone clear.
Furniture models must be finished, not low-detail placeholders; crude slat or box models are not acceptable in a furnished render.
Furniture models must be scaled and detailed appropriately for the room and adjacent pieces; flimsy or out-of-scale models are not acceptable.
A dining table and chairs must not be placed in a narrow window recess that blocks the window; the dining group solver must place the group in a proper dining zone.
Site areas labeled in the documents (pools, terraces, parking) must be built by the site stage; if the outline is not built, the site stage must generate the outline and the model.
Every bedroom must have a door connecting it to the corridor; if the door is missing from the door list, the build stage must add it.

Every room that is not a stair shaft or a shared hall must have at least one door opening in the door list that connects it to a circulation space; if the build stage leaves a furnished room without a door, the run is incomplete and the door must be added from the drawing.
Pieces placed by the decor stage must be preserved by the agent stage; if a piece is missing, the agent must re-place it.
The build stage must preserve every piece the final stage lists; a piece that is in the final list but absent from the built model is a build-stage loss and the stage must be re-run to restore it.

The build stage must preserve every piece the final stage lists in a room; a piece that is in the final list but absent from the built model is a build-stage loss and the stage must be re-run to place it.

The build stage must preserve every piece the final stage lists in a room; a piece that is in the final room's piece list but absent from the built scene is a build-stage loss and the build must be re-run to place it.
A room's listed functional pieces (stove, fridge, sink, cabinets) must be built and visible; if the scene has no object for a planned piece, the build stage failed to place it and must be re-run.
A kitchen run's sink must be built as a distinct fixture on the counter; if the counter is built but the sink is missing from the scene, the build stage failed to place it.
A stair core room whose only camera point is inside the stair must not have its own interior view; the stair is shown from the adjacent hall or landing instead.
A drawn sofa that is dropped by the build stage due to a wall-snap conflict must be re-placed by the build stage at its drawn position or the nearest valid spot; it must not be silently removed.
A drawn sofa that is dropped by the build stage due to a conflict must be re-placed by the build stage at its drawn position or the nearest valid spot; it must not be silently removed.
A drawn floor lamp that is dropped by the build stage due to a conflict must be re-placed by the build stage at its drawn position or the nearest valid spot; it must not be silently removed.
A kitchen sink that is dropped by the build stage due to a conflict must be re-placed by the build stage at its drawn position or the nearest valid spot; it must not be silently removed.
A drawn piece that is dropped by the build stage due to a conflict must be re-placed by the build stage at its drawn position or the nearest valid spot; it must not be silently removed.
A piece that the reading stage typed from the drawing must survive the build stage; if the build drops it, the build stage must re-place it rather than let it vanish.
A drawn block in a kitchen that is not typed must be classified from its size and neighbours before the build stage; an untyped kitchen block is a reading failure, not a valid skip.
Every drawn fixture block on a level must be matched to a model element; a drawn stove with no model counterpart is a reading loss.
Every drawn fixture block on a level must be matched to a model element; a drawn toilet with no model counterpart is a reading loss.
Every drawn fixture block on a level must be matched to a model element; a drawn washbasin with no model counterpart is a reading loss.
Every drawn fixture block on a level must be matched to a model element; a drawn wall cabinet with no model counterpart is a reading loss.
Every drawn fixture block on a level must be matched to a model element; a drawn kitchen sink with no model counterpart is a reading loss.

A drawing layer dedicated to a structural element (stair) that the model already represents must be reconciled: the reading stage must either map its entities to the model element or record why they are redundant, never leave them unaccounted.

A layer whose name names a specific element (stair, door, window) must be read and its entities mapped to that element; if the element is already built from another source, the layer is reconciled against it, not silently dropped.

A kitchen's required appliance set (fridge, stove, sink) must be placed even when the counter run is tight; the solver must allow the fridge to stand at the end of the run or in a corner, and must not drop a required appliance just because the run is crowded.
A bathroom's wet fixtures (bathtub, washbasin, toilet) must not overlap; the fitter must find a non-clashing position before the run is accepted.

A bathtub must be placed so that at least 0.53 m of clear floor remains in front of it; if the drawn bay is too shallow, the fitter must select a shorter tub model or shift the tub to the far end of the bay before the run is accepted.
A toilet's centre must be at least 0.38 m from any side wall or fixture; if the drawn position is too tight, the fitter must select a narrower toilet model or shift it to the nearest valid spot.
An opening must be cut through its wall; if the door ray hits the wall, the opening is not cut and the build stage must re-cut it.
A kitchen counter's top must be at its working height (0.97 m); if the model's top is higher, the build stage must select a model with the correct height.
A frontal view of the entrance facade must be present; if missing, the camera stage must add it.
When the terrain slopes steeper than 1:3, a retaining edge must be built along the slope; the site stage must detect the slope and add the edge.
A railing must have a clear function (guarding an open edge, stair, or balcony); if it stands next to an unexplained hole, the build stage must either remove it or build the feature it guards.
A drawn cluster larger than 4.5 m on a side in a room must be split into individual pieces or marked as a single built-in element, not left untyped.

A drawn piece over 4.5 m on a side in a living room must be resolved into its component furniture (sofa, table, sideboard) or marked as a single built-in before the build stage; it must not be left untyped and unbuilt.

A room whose name and drawn program indicate a children's play/leisure room must be typed 'other' (or a dedicated play type) and furnished with play/leisure pieces, not a full living-room set; a living-room furniture set in a play room is a misread.

When the plan labels a roof terrace with a door to it, the roof build stage must cut an opening over the terrace footprint so the terrace is open to the sky; a closed roof over a labelled terrace is a build error.

A door under a sloped roof whose head would reach over the roof underside must be paired with a dormer or a raised roof line at that wall; a door clipped under the roof is unusable and must be flagged for a dormer.

A site area that is drawn in the plan and rendered in the 3D scene must have its site-area record marked as built with an outline; a 'NOT built (no outline)' record for a rendered pool is a contradiction.
The sheets stage must answer all pending sheet questions before the run is accepted; unanswered questions block the milestone.
A sofa's front must face the long side with the most free space, not the short side; an AI front on the short side is a reading error.
A bench's front must face away from the wall it stands on; an AI front on the short side against a wall is a reading error.
A scene check failure on a built decor item must trigger a re-run of the scene stage for that level before the run is accepted.
The big loop must run enough cycles to raise the house score above the baseline; stopping at the deadline with 0 improvement cycles is a failure.

A tall floor lamp (over 1.4 m) must not be placed in front of a window whose sill is below 0.90 m; the furniture stage must keep the window's sightline and light clear, and the agent must not spend its move budget re-trying a position the code has already refused.
A dining chair must have at least 0.80 m of clear pull-out space behind it; when the room cannot provide it, the furniture stage must drop or re-seat that chair rather than leave a sub-tolerance gap.

A coffee table must not overlap a seating piece; when the drawn coffee table's locked position collides with a drawn armchair, the furniture stage must shrink or re-seat the seating group, not push the locked table.

A wardrobe must have at least 0.80 m of clear opening space in front of it; if the bedroom layout cannot provide it, the wardrobe must be repositioned to a wall with clearance or removed, not left with a 0.15 m gap.

A double bed must have at least 0.60 m of clear walkway on at least one side; when the drawn bed's locked position cannot provide it, the furniture stage must re-seat the bed on a wall span that allows the clearance.

A shoe cabinet must be a finished, detailed model that fits the room's material palette; if the current model is a placeholder, the furniture stage must swap to a library model that passes the fit rules (caps, height) rather than leaving a crude block.

A wardrobe (or any tall storage) must not protrude through the room outline; if the drawn piece extends beyond the wall by more than 0.01 m, the architect rule must flag it as a geometry error, not accept it.
Every seating piece's front use zone must be reachable by a 0.60 m walkway from the room's door; if the walkway is blocked, the architect rule must flag it as an egress/access problem.
A tall floor lamp (over 1.4 m) must not be placed in front of a window whose sill is below 0.90 m; the architect rule must flag any furniture that blocks the window's sightline or light.
A kitchen must include a fridge as part of its functional set; if the kitchen has no fridge, the architect rule must flag it as a missing fixture.
A toilet must have at least 0.38 m of clear space from the side wall or adjacent fixture; if the clearance is less, the architect rule must flag it as a fit problem.
A sofa's front use zone must be free of blocking furniture; if a piece blocks the sofa's viewing or access zone, the architect rule must flag it as a layout problem.
A bedroom window must be dressed with curtains or blinds as part of the room's decor set; if the window is bare, the decor stage must add the missing window treatment.
A dining table and its chairs must not overlap by more than 0.010 m; if the chair cuts into the table by more than tolerance, the furniture stage must re-seat the chair or resize the table.
Fixture models must be finished and detailed, and must match the room's specified material palette; plain boxes or exposed services are not acceptable unless explicitly specified.
A camera for a room must frame the room's main functional group, not a blank wall or partition.
A hall/entry camera must frame the room's defining piece (shoe cabinet, stair) and its function, not a bare corner.
Furniture models must be selected from a coherent style set and must match the room's material palette; generic boxes that do not coordinate with the room are not acceptable.

A living room's seating group (sofa, armchairs) must be dressed with soft layers (cushions, throws) and a rug to match the reference's layered look; bare furniture is not acceptable in a furnished render.
A dining table model must have a finished, textured surface (wood grain, detail) that matches the room's style; a plain, untextured slab is not acceptable.
Dining chairs must be a coherent, curated set that matches the room's style; generic, repetitive, mass-produced models are not acceptable.
A room's render must present a cohesive, warm, layered look (rugs, throws, cohesive lighting) that matches the reference; a chaotic mishmash of styles is not acceptable.
A coffee table must be sized and positioned to function as the anchor of the seating group; a small table floating in open space that blocks the view is not acceptable.
A large, textured rug must anchor the living area; bare wood flooring throughout is not acceptable in a furnished render.
A bathroom camera must frame the room's main functional group (tub, toilet, washbasin) with a wide enough lens to show the ceiling and floor; a tight, low-angle crop of a corner is not acceptable.
A bathroom washbasin must be a modern, clean-lined model that matches the room's style; an ornate, bronze-colored grille is not acceptable.
A bathroom render must present a sophisticated, modern aesthetic that matches the reference; a stark, unfinished utility space with a decorative grille that looks like a prison bar is not acceptable.
A window in a modern bathroom must have a clean, modern frame or glazing; a heavy, ornate metal grille that looks like a security gate is not acceptable.
A bathroom render must present a sophisticated, modern aesthetic that matches the reference; a kitchen-style utility sink and a bizarre, oversized mirror are not acceptable.
A bathroom must be lit with layered, warm lighting (spotlights, cove lighting) to create the mood in the reference; flat, shadowless light is not acceptable.
A nightstand must be a modern, clean-lined model that matches the bed's style; a mid-century modern model with ornate inlay is not acceptable in a minimalist room.

A bedroom render must present a warm, layered style (curtains, art, lamps, styled surfaces) that matches the reference; a bare grey-box with a blank white slab bed and dark block wardrobe is not acceptable.
A nightstand must be a modern, clean-lined model that matches the bed's style; a rustic, distressed model is not acceptable in a minimalist room.
A hall/entry must have warm layered lighting (sconce or pendant); flat grey light is not acceptable in a finished render.
A desk in a bedroom or study must be styled with a lamp and small decor; a bare desk surface is not acceptable in a furnished render.
A bed must be styled with a textured throw and layered bedding; a bare sheet and two pillows is not acceptable in a furnished render.
A camera for a room must frame the room's main functional group, not a door or wall corner.
A bedroom with large windows must have curtains or soft window treatments; bare windows are not acceptable in a furnished render.
A camera for a room must frame the room's main functional group, not a wall or cabinet face.

Bathroom wet surfaces must be finished with the project's tile/stone palette (e.g. large porcelain or zellige on walls, matching stone or tile on the floor); flat untextured grey is not acceptable in a furnished render.

Interior rooms must have warm, layered lighting (e.g. floor lamps, wall sconces, or warm ambient) in the render; flat, dim, or cold single-source lighting is not acceptable.
Living and leisure rooms must have warm, layered lighting (e.g. floor lamps, table lamps, or warm ambient) in the render; a single flat ceiling light is not acceptable.

Outdoor furniture on a balcony or terrace must be a coherent set (matching table and chairs) in a style and material that coordinates with the house's exterior palette; a single dated or mismatched piece is not acceptable.
Paired outdoor furniture (chairs, tables) must use the same model and finish; mismatched chairs or a plain box table are not acceptable on a finished terrace.
Exterior renders must use photorealistic materials, warm directional lighting, and textured landscaping; a flat grey-box massing study with an overcast void is not client-ready.

Exterior facade views must include warm interior light glowing from windows and directional sun or landscape lighting to create depth and a welcoming atmosphere; a flat grey overcast sky with no interior glow is not acceptable.
An exterior camera must frame the house as a whole, showing the main facade, entrance, and roofline; a tight low-angle crop of a corner is not acceptable.
An exterior camera must frame the house as a whole, showing the main facade, entrance, and roofline; a low tight crop of a corner and blank wall is not acceptable.
Exterior renders must show material richness (cladding, lighting, furniture), proper landscaping, and a non-void environment; a grey-box massing study is not client-ready.

Exterior renders must use textured ground, proper paving, and warm directional lighting with material richness; a raw grey-box massing study with flat green ground and bare grid paving is not client-ready.
Drawn furniture in a living room that is untyped must be typed to a plausible type (e.g., sideboard, console_table) based on its size and position; leaving it untyped means nothing builds it.
Decor items must rest on a valid top surface of their host; if no top is found, the agent must re-place the decor or adjust the host geometry.
Decor throws and cushions must not penetrate their host beyond a small tolerance; if the host shows through the cloth, the agent must adjust the placement or model.
Decor cushions must not penetrate their host beyond a small tolerance; if the penetration exceeds the limit, the agent must adjust the placement or model.
Decor throws must have at least 80% of their footprint over the support; if less, the agent must re-place the throw.
Decor cushions must have at least 80% of their footprint over the support; if less, the agent must re-place the cushion.
Decor plants must rest on a valid top surface of their host; if no top is found, the agent must re-place the plant or adjust the host geometry.
Decor throws must not penetrate their host beyond a small tolerance; if the host shows through the cloth, the agent must adjust the placement or model.

Decor items that rest on a host (plant on a table, throw on a sofa) must be placed only on hosts whose built geometry exposes a flat, load-bearing top surface; if the host's top is not found or is recessed, the decor item must be dropped rather than forced into a non-existent surface.

Soft decor items (throws, cushions) must be modeled with a minimum thickness that prevents the host geometry from showing through; if the host's surface is not flat or the item's thickness is less than the host's surface irregularity, the item must be repositioned or removed.
Exterior site items (trees, ground) must use high-quality, photorealistic assets, not low-poly placeholders.
Entities on layers that are off, frozen, or invisible in the source DWG are intentionally excluded from the reading process and do not represent a loss of architectural information.
guards.target: # entities on layers that are off or frozen (or invisible) were not read

guards.rule: OLE2FRAME and WIPEOUT entities are non-geometric or masking entities that do not represent architectural elements and are correctly excluded from the reading process.

When a camera view is dropped during the camera stage, the reason for its removal must be recorded in the ledger; if no reason is given, the view must be retained or the drop must be justified by a specific architectural or technical constraint.

All named blocks in the source DWG that represent architectural elements (e.g., 'bulmak' for a fixture, 'merdiven' for a stair) must be mapped to a corresponding element in the 3D model; if a block is not mapped, the reading stage must flag it for manual review or the building stage must generate a parametric element from its geometry.

Blocks with names starting with 'A$C' are typically auto-generated by CAD software for hatches, dimensions, or other non-architectural entities and do not represent physical elements that need to be mapped to the 3D model.
Drawing blocks that are small symbols, text frames or placeholder inserts with no architectural function must be ignored by the reading stage, not flagged as lost elements.
Auto-generated blocks with the A$C prefix are CAD annotation artifacts and must be excluded from the element ledger.
Site decor elements that are recorded as site decor and not built by design must not be flagged as lost elements.
Drawing blocks that represent elements already built in the model must not be flagged as lost elements.

A drawn block whose name is not in the furniture or fixture dictionary and whose footprint (here ~1.57 x 2.87 m) matches a built-in or storage unit must be typed as a built-in (wardrobe, tall_cabinet or sideboard) in the room it sits in, not dropped as an unrecognised insert.
A drawn block of ~0.6 m square on a floor plan is a small table or stool; the reading stage must type it (side_table or chair) rather than drop it as an unrecognised insert.
A drawn block of ~0.79 m square on a floor plan is a dining or side table; the reading stage must type it (table_dining or side_table) rather than drop it as an unrecognised insert.

Entities on layers that are off or frozen in the source DWG are intentionally hidden by the architect and are not part of the active drawing set; the reading stage is correct to skip them, and this is not a loss.

OLE2FRAME and WIPEOUT entities are non-geometric annotation/occlusion objects (embedded OLE content and whiteout masks) that carry no architectural geometry; the reading stage is correct to skip them, and this is not a loss.

A reading-stage note confirming that a wall layer was selected by strong evidence (rooms closed, strokes paired) is informational, not a loss; columns that stand out of the wall bands are structural elements handled by the structure pass, not furniture to be built.
A drawn symbol that both reading passes classify as not_furniture and that is kept as an obstacle is a deliberate, recorded decision; it is not a lost element and needs no build.

A drawn element on a structural layer (e.g. 'A-BA') that is a column is structure, not furniture; it is correctly excluded from the furniture build and handled by the structure pass, so this is not a loss.

A drawn element that is 60% or more inside an already-built fixture of the same kind is a duplicate drawing (or a part) of that fixture; it is correctly not built a second time, so this is not a loss.
When a drawn symbol is 60% or more inside another symbol of the same type, it is a duplicate or detail of that symbol and must not be built as a separate piece.
When a smaller drawn symbol is inside a larger symbol of the same type, it is a duplicate or detail, not a second piece; only the larger symbol is built.
Layers named '2D', 'Ref', 'Dim', or similar containing only basic entities (lines, circles) are reference layers and are not used for 3D model generation.
Layers containing decorative 2D patterns (tiles, textures) are not used for 3D geometry generation.
Layers containing thin 2D annotations or details (like glass lines) that do not form 3D volumes are not used for 3D geometry generation.
A bench in a room typed as 'other' (like a game/activity room) is likely a misread armchair or chair; retype to a seating type allowed in the room.

When a room outline contains labels for multiple room types (e.g., 'Salon' and 'AÇIK MUTFAK'), the reading stage must identify it as an open-plan space and either split it into sub-zones or assign the primary type while allowing fixtures from the secondary type.
A washbasin model must be fully visible and presented as a functional element in the render; if it is cut off or tiny, swap to a model with better proportions or adjust the camera.
A piece that looks like a tall cabinet in the render but is typed as a fridge should be verified; if it is indeed a fridge, ensure the model is distinct from a tall cabinet.
A dining table model must match the drawn size within tolerance; if it differs, swap to a model with closer dimensions.
An armchair model must match the drawn size within tolerance; if it differs, swap to a model with closer dimensions.

The fitting stage must prefer a library model over a parametric mesh whenever a library model exists for the piece's type and its dimensions fall within the library's size range; a parametric mesh is only acceptable when no library model fits the piece's size and room.

The render stage must use warm ambient lighting (2700-3000K) for interior scenes to create a cozy atmosphere, matching the reference's warm glow; flat, even lighting is not acceptable for a lived-in home.

Door leaves must be built as finished products with visible hardware (handle, hinges) and a surface finish that matches the project's door material slot; a flat, untextured slab is not acceptable in a furnished render.
A conservation check must compare the final stage's piece list against the final model, not against an intermediate build-stage snapshot; a piece present in the final room's piece list is not lost.

A drawn piece in a kitchen or dining zone that is small (under 0.5 m on a side) and sits at counter height in front of a kitchen island or counter must be read as a bar stool, not as a structural column, even if it is drawn on a structure layer; the build stage must not drop it as 'not furniture'.
When a room is a twin of another, the build stage may merge the pair's identical furniture into a single built piece; the twin's duplicate record is then dropped and is not a conservation loss.
When a room is a twin of another, the build stage may merge the pair's identical fixtures into a single built piece; the twin's duplicate record is then dropped and is not a conservation loss.
When the same piece is drawn twice (one outline nested inside the other), the build stage keeps one and drops the duplicate; the dropped record is not a conservation loss.
A piece that the final stage lists must survive the build stage; if a build conflict drops a drawn fixture, the build must re-place it in a valid spot rather than delete it.

A kitchen zone label (e.g. 'AÇIK MUTFAK') inside a living room is an open-plan kitchen, not a misread: keep the room type as living and treat the kitchen pieces as part of the living room's program; do not raise an unhandled zone-label warning.

When a plan labels a room as a terrace or balcony on the top floor and a door leads to it, the roof build stage must cut an opening in the roof over that room to create the outdoor space; a closed roof over a labeled terrace is a build error.

When a door on the top floor under a sloped roof has its head above the roof underside, the reading stage must flag it as requiring a dormer or a roof modification; a door clipped under the roof is not a usable door and must not be built as-is.
A site area the documents label and draw (pool, terrace, parking) must be built as a site element; 'no outline' is a loss, not a valid reason.
A labelled outdoor area (terrace/sunbathing) in the documents must be built; dropping it as 'no outline' loses drawn content.
A labelled parking area in the documents must be built as a site element; 'no outline' is a loss.
Every open-sided stair must be built with a guard/railing on the open side; a bare open stair is a safety defect.
A kitchen must keep at least 0.90 m of aisle in front of the counter and a counter top at working height; a tighter or higher run is a fit failure.
A stove must be a real appliance model flush to its wall; a crude box floating off the wall is a model failure.
A grille or screen in a window slot is a window treatment, not a door; the read stage must not type it as a door.
A door whose height is not drawn must be flagged for review, not silently built at an assumed height.
Site pools and platforms drawn in the plan must be built as 3D elements (water volume, coping, deck) when the site area is labelled.
Labelled outdoor terraces and sunbathing areas must be built as raised decks or paved platforms.
Labelled parking areas must be built as paved surfaces with parking lines.
When the site plan draws a pool or a sunning terrace, the site stage must build them as site areas with their paving and furniture, not leave them as 'NOT built'.
A large room on the top floor of a house that is labelled as a relaxation or activity room and has no other function should be typed as a bedroom, not 'other'.
A shoe cabinet should only be placed at the entrance hall (ground floor), not in a top floor hall.

the judge scores view cam_r_L1_oyun_aktivite_ve_dinlenme_odasi_1 2/5 (a client would not accept it): The render is a plain, low-budget living room that fails the standard set by the reference. The furniture is a mismatched set of two different brown sofas and a heavy, dark coffee table that clashes with the light floor. The room is missing the key styling layers seen in the reference: a feature wall, wall art, and a warm, layered lighting scheme. The large window looks out onto a flat, empty field, which makes the space feel unfinished and un-stylish.
missing layer: styled surfaces. The heavy, dark wood coffee table is a third, clashing material and style that does not go with the light floor or the brown sofas, making the set look disjointed.

missing layer: a warm light. The room is lit by a single, flat ceiling light, creating a cold and uninviting atmosphere. It lacks the warm, layered lighting (like the chandelier in the reference) that makes a space feel designed.
also: Mismatched furniture set. The room contains at least three different styles of seating: a modern brown sofa (f_L1_017), a different, more traditional-looking sofa (f_L1_020), and a third distinct sofa/armchair in the foreground. They do not form a coherent group.

findings.message: missing layer: wall art. The large, blank wall behind the sofa is a major flaw. It lacks any feature, such as the textured wall and clock seen in the reference, leaving the main focal point of the room empty and unfinished.
also: The view through the window and over the railing is a flat, untextured green field with lollipop trees. This 'flat outdoor' environment makes the render look unfinished and unconvincing.
The view outside the window is a flat, empty green field with simple, lollipop-like trees. This makes the render look unfinished and unappealing.

findings.message: The two sofas are of different models and proportions, creating a mismatched set that looks like a collection of random pieces rather than a coordinated design.
also: mismatched_set: the dark brown sofa (f_L1_020) clashes with the lighter tan sofa (f_L1_017) in the same room; they are different styles and colours that do not form a coherent set.

findings.message: missing layer: dining set. The room is defined as a game/activity/leisure room and the JSON includes a dining table and chairs, but they are absent from the render, leaving the space incomplete.

the judge scores view ext_1 2/5 (a client would not accept it): The render is a flat, grey-box style massing study, not a client-ready image. The lighting is a dead, overcast grey that makes the white facade look dirty and the stone cladding muddy. The landscaping is a flat green plane with no texture, and the entire scene lacks the warm, styled, and detailed finish (warm light, planters, furniture, rich materials) that the reference photo sets as the standard for this project.

missing layer: warm light. The entire facade is lit by a flat, grey, overcast sky. There is no warm interior light glowing from the windows, no landscape lighting, and no sun to create depth and a welcoming atmosphere, making the house look cold and unfinished.
also: missing layer: planters. The ground is a flat, untextured green plane. There are no planters, beds, or defined landscaping elements to soften the transition between the building and the ground, which is a key feature of the reference style.

missing layer: a place to sit. The outdoor space is completely empty. There is no patio furniture, bench, or any indication of how the outdoor living space is meant to be used, making it feel like a void rather than a designed area.

missing layer: lanterns. There are no exterior light fixtures (wall sconces, bollard lights, or path lights) visible on the facade or in the landscape. This is a critical omission for a modern home, both for function and for the 'styled' look required for a client presentation.

missing layer: a rug. While less critical outdoors, the complete lack of any ground-covering element (like a large outdoor rug or pavers) in front of the main glass wall makes the space feel incomplete and un-styled.
missing layer: warm wood accents. The reference uses rich timber cladding to break up the white walls and add warmth. This render is entirely white stucco and stone, making it look cold and generic.

missing layer: outdoor lighting. The reference has bollard lights and landscape lighting that define the paths and add ambiance. This render has no exterior lighting fixtures visible, making the outdoor space feel unfinished.

missing layer: styled planters. The reference has deliberate, high-quality planters and hardscaping elements. This render has a generic hedge and bare grass, lacking the curated landscaping of the project style.
missing layer: warm light. The interior of the reference glows with warm light, suggesting a lived-in space. The windows here are dark and flat, offering no sense of interior life or warmth.
missing layer: a place to sit. The terrace and pool deck are completely empty, lacking the outdoor furniture and loungers that would make the space feel livable and complete.
missing layer: planters. The reference shows a rich landscape with varied planting; this render has only a few crude, low-poly hedge blocks that look like placeholders.
missing layer: a warm light. The scene is lit by a flat, hazy daylight with no architectural lighting, downlights, or warm interior glow to define the home's character.
missing layer: styled surfaces. The ground is a single, untextured green plane and the paving is a generic grey, lacking the material variety (stone, wood, gravel) of a designed landscape.

The overall aesthetic is a 'grey box' massing model. The walls are flat white and the stone cladding is a simple texture, missing the layered materials, roof details, and crisp architectural lines of the reference.

missing layer: styled surfaces. The entire facade is a flat, untextured white and brown block. It lacks the warm timber cladding, stone, and material contrast seen in the reference, making it look like a placeholder.

missing layer: plants. The site is completely bare. There is no landscaping, no planters, no trees, and no greenery to soften the building or define the outdoor space, unlike the lush lawn and trees in the reference.
missing layer: a place to sit. The outdoor area is a vast, empty paved slab. There is no patio furniture, no bench, and no defined living zone, making the exterior feel uninhabited and uninviting.

missing layer: a warm light. The lighting is flat, grey, and unflattering. It fails to create the welcoming, high-contrast atmosphere of the reference photo, which uses bright daylight and clear shadows to make the house pop.
missing layer: lanterns. There is no exterior lighting (path lights, wall sconces, or lanterns) to define the walkways or add architectural detail at night, a key element of a well-designed exterior.

missing layer: a warm light. The scene is lit by a flat, grey, overcast sky. There is no warm light from windows or exterior fixtures to make the house feel inviting and finished.

rules_proposed.rule: A level whose rooms survive into the final stage must have its full wall set and door openings rebuilt by the build stage; if a level's walls are dropped, the build stage must be re-run to reconstruct them from the drawing rather than leaving the level's rooms open.

The build stage must cut every door, window and opening the reading stage placed on a wall; an opening that exists in the reading but is absent from the built walls is a build failure, not a reading error.
Every site area the documents label (parking, terrace, pool) must be built as a modelled outdoor space with its outline; a labelled site area left unbuilt with no reason is a site-stage loss.
Every room the documents name with a label and area must be created in the model; a named room with no matching model room is a reading-stage loss.
none
The build stage must not drop furniture that the final stage places; every piece present in the final stage must be carried through the build stage.
The build stage must preserve every furniture piece placed by the final stage; if a piece is missing after build, the build stage must be re-run to restore it.
Pieces placed by the decor stage must be preserved by the build stage; if a piece is missing, the build stage must re-place it.
A room's listed functional pieces (stove, fridge, cabinets) must be built and visible; if the render shows an empty shell, the build stage failed to place them.
A dedicated stair room whose only camera point is inside the stair core must be shown from the adjacent hall, not given its own interior view.
A drawn piece that is read as unknown must be typed or marked with evidence before the run is accepted; it may not be left untyped and unbuilt without a record.
A drawn block that names a fixture (stove, toilet, etc.) must be added to the model as that fixture; a drawn fixture with no model element is a loss.

A drawn fixture block that falls inside a room the model has already furnished with the same fixture type is a duplicate ledger entry, not a lost piece; the reading stage must match drawn blocks to already-built pieces by room and type before flagging them as lost.

A small wall cabinet drawn inside a bathroom that is already furnished as a complete wet set is an optional accessory; the ledger must not flag it as a lost major piece when the room's core fixtures are present.
In an open-plan room where the kitchen zone is already furnished, a drawn kitchen sink block that falls within that zone is a duplicate of the built sink, not a lost piece.
A drawn stove block inside a room that already has a built stove is a duplicate ledger entry, not a lost piece.
A drawn toilet block inside a bathroom that already has a built toilet is a duplicate ledger entry, not a lost piece.
A drawn washbasin block inside a bathroom that already has a built washbasin is a duplicate ledger entry, not a lost piece.
A small wall cabinet drawn inside a fully furnished bathroom is an optional accessory; the ledger must not flag it as a lost major piece.
A drawn kitchen sink block inside a room that already has a built kitchen sink is a duplicate ledger entry, not a lost piece.

A stair layer whose geometry is consumed by a built stair piece must be linked to that piece in the ledger; an unlinked stair layer is a false 'lost' finding when the stair is already present in the model.
Stair elevation layers are reference views of an already-built stair; they must not be flagged as lost 3D elements.
A decorative sanitary-ware layer whose geometry corresponds to already-built bathroom fixtures must be linked to those pieces; it is not a separate lost element.
A sanitary-ware detail layer whose geometry corresponds to already-built fixtures must be linked to those pieces; it is not a separate lost element.

A small drawn symbol that sits mostly inside a larger drawn piece of the same type in the same room is a double-drawn symbol of that one piece, not a second piece; the reading must keep the larger one and drop the inner duplicate.

A drawn piece that an AI pass has named and whose size fits that name must be built as that named piece, even when it is drawn overlapping a larger piece; the overlap is a drawing offset, not a reason to drop it as a detail.
Entities on layers that are off, frozen or invisible in the source DWG are not part of the issued drawing and must not be read; the ledger must not flag them as lost.
OLE2FRAME and WIPEOUT entities are annotation/occlusion graphics, not building geometry or furniture, and must not be read as pieces; the ledger must not flag them as lost.

A camera view that exists in the baseline must not be dropped by a later stage without a recorded reason; if a view is removed, the stage must state why, and an exterior view of the building is never dropped silently.

A named block instance in the source (a block with a meaningful name such as a fixture or furniture label) that the model does not use must be traced to a built element or explicitly marked as not furniture with evidence; it must not be silently ignored.
AutoCAD anonymous block names (A$C...) are internal geometry fragments (hatches, dimension arrows, small symbols) and must not be flagged as lost building elements.
Unlabeled, generic CAD blocks (e.g., 'eeere', 'A$C...') that do not correspond to a named architectural element or fixture are not required to be built; they are drawing artifacts.
Tiny anonymous CAD blocks (A$C...) under 0.1 m are annotation or dimension artifacts and are not built.
Blocks with random alphanumeric names that do not match known fixture or furniture types are treated as drawing artifacts and not built.
Generic CAD blocks without clear architectural labels are not built unless they match a known fixture or furniture type.
Site decor elements are not built as part of the interior or exterior architectural model; they are recorded for reference only.
Stair blocks in the drawing are represented by the built stair elements in the model; duplicate stair blocks are not built separately.
Tiny anonymous CAD blocks (A$C...) under 0.3 m are annotation or dimension artifacts and are not built.
Tiny anonymous CAD blocks (A$C...) under 0.2 m are annotation or dimension artifacts and are not built.

A drawn block whose name is not in the furniture or fixture catalogue and whose footprint does not match a known piece must be classified as a built-in or structural element and built as such, not silently dropped from the model.

A conservation 'gone after build' finding on a drawn fixture id is a false alarm when the final room inventory of the same room still lists a piece of that type; the build stage re-solves drawn zones and re-ids the members, so the check must match by type and zone, not by the original drawn id.

A drawn mark that was never verified to a furniture type and is not part of the room's functional program may be dropped by the build stage without being a conservation loss; only typed, program-required pieces count as lost.

A conservation 'gone after build' finding on a stair id is a false alarm when the final room inventory of the stair's hall still lists a stair; the warning text describing landing depth is a reading note, not evidence of loss.
A drawn element on a structure layer (e.g. 'A-BA') that the code classifies as a column or structural member is not furniture and may be dropped by the build stage without being a conservation loss.

A drawn element on a structural layer (A-BA) is a building element, not furniture; it is kept as an obstacle and not built as a piece.
Furniture symbols on a dedicated furniture layer are placed by the furniture agent, not the build stage; the build stage correctly leaves them for the agent.
Elements on a decor layer are placed by the decor stage, not the build stage; the build stage correctly leaves them for the decor stage.
Drawn elements that are 60% or more inside a larger fixture are parts of that fixture, not separate pieces; they are not built separately.
Exterior site areas (parking, terrace, pool) are built as site surfaces (paving, grass, water), not as individual furniture pieces; the build stage correctly handles them at the site level.
Drawn details inside a kitchen counter (appliance fronts, drawers) are parts of the counter module, not separate pieces; they are not built separately.
A drawn cluster larger than 4.5 m on a side is a group of pieces; the build stage leaves it for the furniture agent to split or place as a built-in.
A drawn symbol that both recognition passes classify as not_furniture is kept as an obstacle and not built as a piece.
A drawn outline around a table and its chairs that is 78% or more of its box is a rug mark, not a furniture piece; the decor stage places the rug.
Cushions and pillows that are part of a sofa or chair model are not separate decor pieces; they are included in the model.
Two floor lamps that overlap by 30% or more are one lamp drawn twice; the larger footprint is kept and the smaller is not built.
Two floor lamps that overlap by 15% or more are one lamp drawn twice; the larger footprint is kept and the smaller is not built.
When two pieces of the same type overlap by more than 10% and are of similar size, the recognition stage must treat them as a single drawn element and keep only the larger or more complete one.
A small outline (under 0.5 m) drawn 80% or more inside a larger seat piece is its cushion or part, not a separate ottoman; the recognition stage must not type it as independent furniture.
A large outline (over 2 m on a side) that encloses other furniture pieces is a rug or zone boundary, not a piece; the build stage must not attempt to build it as furniture.
A stair's upper landing on the top floor is not a separate piece to be built; it is the arrival point of the stair from the floor below.
Every level present in the plan with rooms and openings must have its walls and openings built; a level whose walls are all missing after the build stage is a build failure, not a reading choice.
Every room the documents name with a label and area must be matched to a model room; a named room with no model room using it is a reading-stage loss.
A room label in the documents that matches an already-built room by position and function is not a lost room; the ledger must not flag it as missing.
Pieces placed by the decor stage must be preserved by the agent stage; if a piece is missing, the agent must re-place it.
The build stage must preserve every piece the final stage lists; a piece that is in the final list but absent from the built model is a build-stage loss and the stage must be re-run to restore it.

The build stage must preserve every piece the final stage lists in a room; a piece that is in the final list but absent from the built model is a build-stage loss and the stage must be re-run to place it.

The build stage must preserve every piece the final stage lists in a room; a piece that is in the final room's piece list but absent from the built scene is a build-stage loss and the build must be re-run to place it.
A room's listed functional pieces (stove, fridge, sink, cabinets) must be built and visible; if the scene has no object for a planned piece, the build stage failed to place it and must be re-run.
A kitchen run's sink must be built as a distinct fixture on the counter; if the counter is built but the sink is missing from the scene, the build stage failed to place it.
A stair core room whose only camera point is inside the stair must not have its own interior view; the stair is shown from the adjacent hall or landing instead.
A drawn sofa that is dropped by the build stage due to a wall-snap conflict must be re-placed by the build stage at its drawn position or the nearest valid spot; it must not be silently removed.
A drawn sofa that is dropped by the build stage due to a conflict must be re-placed by the build stage at its drawn position or the nearest valid spot; it must not be silently removed.
A drawn floor lamp that is dropped by the build stage due to a conflict must be re-placed by the build stage at its drawn position or the nearest valid spot; it must not be silently removed.
A kitchen sink that is dropped by the build stage due to a conflict must be re-placed by the build stage at its drawn position or the nearest valid spot; it must not be silently removed.
A drawn piece that is dropped by the build stage due to a conflict must be re-placed by the build stage at its drawn position or the nearest valid spot; it must not be silently removed.
A piece that the reading stage typed from the drawing must survive the build stage; if the build drops it, the build stage must re-place it rather than let it vanish.
A drawn block in a kitchen that is not typed must be classified from its size and neighbours before the build stage; an untyped kitchen block is a reading failure, not a valid skip.
Every drawn fixture block on a level must be matched to a model element; a drawn stove with no model counterpart is a reading loss.
Every drawn fixture block on a level must be matched to a model element; a drawn toilet with no model counterpart is a reading loss.
Every drawn fixture block on a level must be matched to a model element; a drawn washbasin with no model counterpart is a reading loss.
Every drawn fixture block on a level must be matched to a model element; a drawn wall cabinet with no model counterpart is a reading loss.
Every drawn fixture block on a level must be matched to a model element; a drawn kitchen sink with no model counterpart is a reading loss.

A drawing layer dedicated to a structural element (stair) that the model already represents must be reconciled: the reading stage must either map its entities to the model element or record why they are redundant, never leave them unaccounted.

A layer whose name names a specific element (stair, door, window) must be read and its entities mapped to that element; if the element is already built from another source, the layer is reconciled against it, not silently dropped.
Entities on layers that are off, frozen, or invisible in the source DWG are intentionally excluded from the reading process and do not represent a loss of architectural information.
OLE2FRAME and WIPEOUT entities are non-geometric or masking entities that do not represent architectural elements and are correctly excluded from the reading process.

When a camera view is dropped during the camera stage, the reason for its removal must be recorded in the ledger; if no reason is given, the view must be retained or the drop must be justified by a specific architectural or technical constraint.

All named blocks in the source DWG that represent architectural elements (e.g., 'bulmak' for a fixture, 'merdiven' for a stair) must be mapped to a corresponding element in the 3D model; if a block is not mapped, the reading stage must flag it for manual review or the building stage must generate a parametric element from its geometry.

Blocks with names starting with 'A$C' are typically auto-generated by CAD software for hatches, dimensions, or other non-architectural entities and do not represent physical elements that need to be mapped to the 3D model.
Drawing blocks that are small symbols, text frames or placeholder inserts with no architectural function must be ignored by the reading stage, not flagged as lost elements.
Auto-generated blocks with the A$C prefix are CAD annotation artifacts and must be excluded from the element ledger.
Site decor elements that are recorded as site decor and not built by design must not be flagged as lost elements.
Drawing blocks that represent elements already built in the model must not be flagged as lost elements.

A drawn block whose name is not in the furniture or fixture dictionary and whose footprint (here ~1.57 x 2.87 m) matches a built-in or storage unit must be typed as a built-in (wardrobe, tall_cabinet or sideboard) in the room it sits in, not dropped as an unrecognised insert.
A drawn block of ~0.6 m square on a floor plan is a small table or stool; the reading stage must type it (side_table or chair) rather than drop it as an unrecognised insert.
A drawn block of ~0.79 m square on a floor plan is a dining or side table; the reading stage must type it (table_dining or side_table) rather than drop it as an unrecognised insert.

Entities on layers that are off or frozen in the source DWG are intentionally hidden by the architect and are not part of the active drawing set; the reading stage is correct to skip them, and this is not a loss.

OLE2FRAME and WIPEOUT entities are non-geometric annotation/occlusion objects (embedded OLE content and whiteout masks) that carry no architectural geometry; the reading stage is correct to skip them, and this is not a loss.

A reading-stage note confirming that a wall layer was selected by strong evidence (rooms closed, strokes paired) is informational, not a loss; columns that stand out of the wall bands are structural elements handled by the structure pass, not furniture to be built.
A drawn symbol that both reading passes classify as not_furniture and that is kept as an obstacle is a deliberate, recorded decision; it is not a lost element and needs no build.

A drawn element on a structural layer (e.g. 'A-BA') that is a column is structure, not furniture; it is correctly excluded from the furniture build and handled by the structure pass, so this is not a loss.

A drawn element that is 60% or more inside an already-built fixture of the same kind is a duplicate drawing (or a part) of that fixture; it is correctly not built a second time, so this is not a loss.
When a drawn symbol is 60% or more inside another symbol of the same type, it is a duplicate or detail of that symbol and must not be built as a separate piece.
When a smaller drawn symbol is inside a larger symbol of the same type, it is a duplicate or detail, not a second piece; only the larger symbol is built.
Layers named '2D', 'Ref', 'Dim', or similar containing only basic entities (lines, circles) are reference layers and are not used for 3D model generation.
Layers containing decorative 2D patterns (tiles, textures) are not used for 3D geometry generation.
Layers containing thin 2D annotations or details (like glass lines) that do not form 3D volumes are not used for 3D geometry generation.
A conservation check must compare the final stage's piece list against the final model, not against an intermediate build-stage snapshot; a piece present in the final room's piece list is not lost.

A drawn piece in a kitchen or dining zone that is small (under 0.5 m on a side) and sits at counter height in front of a kitchen island or counter must be read as a bar stool, not as a structural column, even if it is drawn on a structure layer; the build stage must not drop it as 'not furniture'.
When a room is a twin of another, the build stage may merge the pair's identical furniture into a single built piece; the twin's duplicate record is then dropped and is not a conservation loss.
When a room is a twin of another, the build stage may merge the pair's identical fixtures into a single built piece; the twin's duplicate record is then dropped and is not a conservation loss.
When the same piece is drawn twice (one outline nested inside the other), the build stage keeps one and drops the duplicate; the dropped record is not a conservation loss.
A piece that the final stage lists must survive the build stage; if a build conflict drops a drawn fixture, the build must re-place it in a valid spot rather than delete it.
A site area the documents label and draw (pool, terrace, parking) must be built as a site element; 'no outline' is a loss, not a valid reason.
A labelled outdoor area (terrace/sunbathing) in the documents must be built; dropping it as 'no outline' loses drawn content.
A labelled parking area in the documents must be built as a site element; 'no outline' is a loss.
When the site plan draws a pool or a sunning terrace, the site stage must build them as site areas with their paving and furniture, not leave them as 'NOT built'.
